notes: Cool Andes nights keep acidity high alongside ripe fruit from long, sunny days.
Carmenère is one of Chile's emblematic reds, with intense color and notes of red fruit, damp earth and spice.
Casablanca is a cool, ocean-influenced valley whose leading grapes are Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay.
Colchagua makes mostly red wine, particularly Carmenère, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.
Pacific breezes cool the valley and lengthen ripening, helping the grapes keep their acidity.
Curicó is one of Chile's largest wine areas, and Cabernet Sauvignon and Sauvignon Blanc are its main grapes.
Maipo Cabernet Sauvignon is marked by pervasive blackcurrant fruit and an earthy, dusty note.
Maule is Chile's largest wine region, and its Carmenère is notably spicy, with black pepper.
Old Carignan vines give soft, earthy reds with rich plum and black fruit.
Newer plantings of Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Carmenère show bright acidity and juicy fruit.
Limarí is best known for Chardonnay and Syrah, and it also makes Pinot Noir.
Morning fog from the Pacific and mineral-rich soils give fresh wines with a distinct mineral edge.
Southern Chile is cool and wet. Its newer vineyards suit Pinot Noir, Chardonnay, Sauvignon Blanc and Riesling, and Itata keeps old País and Muscat vines.
The Andes and Coastal Range trap warm, dry air here, while cool Andes nights keep acidity high alongside ripe fruit.
Elqui is arid, with clear skies, and Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc lead.
In its cool climate, Syrah becomes spicy and complex.
In the Elqui Valley, Syrah and Sauvignon Blanc lead, and the cool climate makes Syrah spicy and complex.
The Limarí Valley's limestone soils and sea breezes give Chardonnay an attractive minerality.
Limarí Syrah is also well regarded.
Cachapoal is known for reds, mainly Carmenère, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, about 80% of its output.
Cool-climate grapes grow in high vineyards in the Andes foothills, and warmer ones near Lake Rapel.
Bright sun, Andes breezes and cool nights give Cabernet Sauvignon consistent ripeness.
